transcript.content: Hi, welcome in. I'm Dr. Smith. Can you tell me what brings you in to see me today?

Hi, Dr. Smith. Um… I guess what finally pushed me to make the appointment is that I keep not finishing things I really do intend to finish. Like after audits, or after mentorship events at work, there are always these follow-up items—sending the final email, putting in a review note, filling out a form, just closing the loop basically. And I’ll start them, or I’ll mentally mark them as “almost done,” and then a few days later I find out that the last step never actually happened.

It’s embarrassing, because these aren’t things I don’t care about. I’ll have every intention of doing them, and sometimes I even remember starting them, so in my head they feel completed. But then there’s no sent email, or the note is still sitting unfinished, or the form was never submitted. It’s gotten to the point where I don’t feel like I can just chalk it up to being busy, and I thought I should talk to someone about it.
Would you say you've had this kind of trouble finishing tasks and follow-up steps since you were a kid or in school, or is this a new pattern that's really only shown up recently?

No, it’s definitely not new. I mean, it’s showing up in a more serious way now because work has so many little closing-the-loop steps, but when I think back, it was there really early.

Even in elementary school my report cards would say things like I was bright, or I understood the material, but I lost assignments, rushed through and missed small details, talked out of turn, needed reminders to finish work. It was kind of a running theme. My mother still jokes that I could ace the test on the book or the lesson, but the actual project would be sitting in my backpack, completely done or half-done, and I just wouldn’t turn it in. Or I’d forget it existed once it wasn’t right in front of me.

So… yeah, I don’t think this is something that just started recently. I think I got better at compensating in some ways, but the pattern was there when I was a kid.
Besides the trouble finishing tasks, have you noticed things like feeling restless or fidgety, having a hard time sitting still, or blurting things out or acting impulsively, both as a kid and now?

Yes, definitely the restless part. I don’t know if I would have called it that when I was younger, but sitting still for a long time has always felt… uncomfortable in a very physical way. Like if I’m in a long review meeting at work, especially one where I’m supposed to just sit there and listen or go through documents line by line, it feels like this pressure starts building up inside me.

It’s not just boredom exactly. It’s more like my body is saying, “You need to move now.” I’ll start looking for a reason to get up—walking to the printer, getting water, offering to grab something, checking whether something printed even if I don’t really need it right then. Sometimes I’ll invent a little errand just so I can stand up and reset for a minute.

And as a kid, I remember that same feeling in class or assemblies, though I didn’t have the words for it. I just knew sitting there quietly felt almost impossible after a while. Even now, I can make myself do it because I’m an adult and I know I’m supposed to, but it takes a lot of effort, and internally I’m really fighting the urge to get up and move.
Do you often find yourself interrupting others, finishing their sentences, or blurting out answers or comments before someone has finished speaking—and was that true when you were a child as well?

Yes… I do. I wish I didn’t, because I know it can come across as rude or like I’m not listening, and that’s not how I mean it. It’s more like the answer or the idea pops into my head and it feels urgent, like if I don’t say it right then I’m going to lose it or the conversation is going to go the wrong direction.

It happens a lot at work, especially with junior auditors. If someone is explaining an issue or walking through what they found, I’ll catch myself jumping in before they’ve actually finished. I’ll finish the thought for them, or I’ll say, “Right, so what you need to do is…” before they’ve gotten to the part where they were maybe going to say that themselves. And sometimes I can see on their face that I cut them off, and then I feel terrible and try to back up and say, “Sorry, keep going.” But the blurting happens before I’ve really made a conscious decision to speak.

As a kid, yes, I think that was there too. I was the kid who would call out an answer if I knew it, or jump into conversations because I thought I knew where someone was going. I don’t think I experienced it as interrupting at the time—I just felt like I was participating, or excited, or like the thought needed to come out right away. But looking back, yes, that pattern has definitely been there for a long time.
Do these same difficulties—forgetting to finish things, feeling restless, or interrupting—also cause problems for you outside of work, like at home or in your personal relationships?

Yes, it definitely isn’t just work. Work is where it’s most visible right now because there are consequences and other people are checking the details, but it spills over at home too.

At work, the unfinished follow-up has gotten embarrassing, honestly. It’s not just “oh, I misplaced a note” anymore. I’ve missed or delayed little closing steps after reviews, or thought I had responded to something when I hadn’t, and it affected a client review. That really scared me, because I’ve worked hard to get where I am, and now I’m in this position where I’m worried people are quietly wondering if I can actually handle the promotion or if I’m not as reliable as they thought. And I hate that, because I do care. I’m not being careless on purpose.

At home, my husband has basically taken over certain things because he doesn’t trust that I’ll complete them consistently. Bills are a big one, and also commitments I agree to—like paperwork, appointments, things we said we’d take care of. I’ll say, “Yes, I’ll do that,” and I fully mean it in the moment, but then it either falls out of my head or I start it and don’t finish the last step. So he ends up stepping in, not because he wants to control everything, but because if he doesn’t, something may not get done. That causes tension, because I feel ashamed and defensive, and he feels like he can’t count on me.

So yes, it’s not contained to one area. It’s affecting both my work and my marriage, and that’s part of why I’m here.
